svg.aria-label: Diagram: users, groups and administrative units in Microsoft Entra ID, showing what object types each container can hold, four documented rules where containment does not behave as inheritance, what an administrative unit scoped administrator can and cannot do to a group inside it, and the restrictions on role-assignable groups including the immutable isAssignableToRole flag and the limit of 500 per tenant
svg.title: Four containers in Entra ID — three of them cannot nest at all, and the one that can does not pass access down
svg.text: In Azure, a container implies inheritance. In Entra, mostly it does not.
Management groups nest six deep and push policy downward. These four containers each stop the inheritance somewhere, and each stops it differently.
First, what each container is even allowed to hold
Security group
users, devices, service principals — and other groups. Owned by users or service principals.
Microsoft 365 group
users only — and people outside your organization can be members.
Administrative unit
only users, groups, or devices. Not service principals, and not other administrative units.
Role-assignable group
members, but never another group. Membership type must be Assigned, never dynamic.
Then, the four places containment stops — each documented, none obvious
A group inside a group
“only members in the parent group have access to shared resources and applications”
A group inside an AU
brings “the group itself into the management scope … but not the members of the group”
An AU inside an AU
“Administrative units can’t be nested.” One level, and that is the whole hierarchy.
A group inside a role-assignable group
“Group nesting isn’t supported.” Not a caveat — a refusal.
Compare Phase 1: a management group tree supports six levels and policy assigned at the top is inherited by everything beneath it.
A User Administrator scoped to an AU
holding a group, on that group’s members:
CAN
manage the name of the group
manage the membership of the group
CANNOT
manage user properties of members
manage their authentication methods
reset their passwords
To do those, add the users to the AU directly.
And the default that undoes the whole point
“If you assign a role to a user that is not a member of
an administrative unit, the scope of the role is the
entire tenant.”
The failure is silent. A delegation that was meant to
cover one faculty covers the directory, and nothing in
the portal announces the difference.
AU scope also applies only to management permissions.
It does not stop anyone browsing outside the unit.
The one container you must get right at creation, because it cannot be changed after
Role-assignable groups
isAssignableToRole
is immutable
— settable only
on new groups. You can’t convert an existing group.
maximum per tenant — a budget, like the 4,000
role assignments of post #18.
Privileged Role Administrator to create. Membership
Assigned only. Soft-deleted, restorable for 30 days.
Why the restrictions exist, in their own words
“An Exchange administrator who can modify dynamic
membership groups could add themselves to the
Contoso_User_Administrators group and in that way
become a User Administrator.”
That is the reason dynamic membership is banned here.
A rule that writes membership is a rule that writes
privilege, and the rule has its own editors.
Sources: Learn about groups, Administrative units in Microsoft Entra ID, and Use Microsoft Entra groups to manage role assignments, on Microsoft Learn.
